articles.text: With all the hype surrounding elections, the Murphy family created a simple message of hope nearly two months prior to the November 3 Presidential election. Their message on a blue handmade sign on their front lawn read: “Make America Respectable Again.” Created by dad, Zach Murphy, and younger daughter Ella, 14, they installed the sign in front of their house on Oakland Avenue. Ella explained that the message simply calls for political decency. “We’re not really there right now,” she said this week. The message was an obvious twist on President Trump’s 2016 campaign slogan to Make America Great Again, and was painted in a bright blue rather than Trump’s red. Explaining the sign’s history, Zach said that both daughters, Ella and older sister Claire, walked around Piedmont in September, trying to count lawn signs for presidential candidates to see how Piedmonters would be voting in November. While there were many signs showing support for School Board and City Council candidates, there were far fewer signs showing support for either presidential candidate. “They were surprised to see very few national [campaign] signs. We started talking about what message we could put out there that would hopefully encourage people to aim for something attainable,” Zach said with a smile. Since the sign went up, both Ella and Zach have confirmed a neighborhood interest in the message and have noticed people taking photos of it and people walking by taking “selfies” with the sign. Given the negative advertising that accompanies most elections, their message was seen as one of optimism. It was the only one of its type in the city.

articles.text: Last week, the Post published an article on the Mental Health Screener, a survey sent to all Piedmont students on September 30. Results were not released until mid-December to the public. This week, parents weighed in on the results, the screener itself and what they have noticed about the mental health of Piedmont students. They expressed an urgent need for School Superintendent Randy Booker and Curriculum Director Cheryl Wozniak to clarify the survey results in a comprehensible way and to address the current stress level of students at most grade levels. Alisa Crovetti, the Clinical Supervisor Psychologist at the school district’s Wellness Center and a Piedmont mom, was a consultant in the early stages before the mental health survey was sent out. She later became involved again when the data was made available. Crovetti wants to use a criterion-referenced screener rather than a norm-referenced screener on surveys in the future. She made that recommendation to the team of 18 that designed the screener once the initial results came back in October. “No screener can be diagnostic, but a criterion referenced screener may feel a lot more intuitive for the community. It would allow us to identify kids who fall into ‘extreme’ or ‘severe’ categories of symptomology. It’s very challenging to find a criterion-referenced tool that is appropriate for all age levels,” she added. Piedmont parent Laura Maestrelli took action on the mental health topic in October by conducting an informal anonymous survey of Piedmont students. The comments received from students after only two months of distance learning were harrowing, and she read the student comments aloud at a School Board meeting on October 26. articles.text: One of the biggest understatements in the Bible might well be the statement of Jesus in the Gospel of John when He said: “In the world you will have tribulation.” It’s pretty hard to argue the truth of that statement. A quick look at local, national, and world events, not to mention taking stock of our own personal challenges, reminds us that in the world we have tribulation – and plenty of it. But Jesus put His statement about tribulation in the world into the context of the promises of His grace. He prefaced His statement by saying: “I have said these things to you, that in Me you may have peace.” Jesus was saying: “I know that tribulation is rampant. And I know it causes anxiety, discouragement, frustration, and stress of all kinds. But I am giving you My promises so that You may have My peace!” Jesus said: “In the world you will have tribulation. But take heart!” Literally that means to be confidant, to be courageous, and to be strong. It doesn’t imply the absence of fear, but it limits the power of fear by pointing to a rock-solid reason for confidence, for hope, and for victory. Jesus continued, “I have overcome the world.” Jesus overcame the world by conquering sin and guilt through His own death and by rising again in glorious victory over all the forces of evil in this life and in the life to come. Amelie Kappes, Colleen Allan, and Teebie Saunders, Co-Chairs of this year’s Piedmont Education Foundation Giving Campaign, announced that the Giving Campaign’s $3,000,000 fundraising goal has been exceeded. The Giving Campaign is the largest annual fundraiser supporting the students and schools of Piedmont. This success came amidst a year of multiple challenges. “We set this lofty goal during a year of distance learning with no reopening timeline amid a coronavirus surge in the country, and when our district was facing issues of unprecedented scale and complexity,” said Allan. “This is a true testament to the value that our community places on the importance of a strong public school district and a topnotch education for Piedmont students.” The campaign, launched on September 21, went for 15 weeks. Kappes credits the work of the community for the strength of this year’s campaign. “It reflects untold hours of volunteer support and a team of thoughtful, strategic, dedicated and engaged staff at the PEF office. PUSD will benefit across all campuses as a result of this generosity, involvement and hard work.” More than 75 volunteers and staff members engaged in this effort, which included multiple forms of outreach as part of the overall strategy of personally reaching out to as many prospective donors as possible. This year’s total of $3,014,210 is an amount surpassed only once in the Campaign’s long history. The number of participants, however, was down. The participation rate among parents, which has been at about 68% for the past few years, dropped to 57% this year. Saunders suggested there were multiple reasons, “We are truly grateful to the 1,140 families that contributed to this year’s Giving Campaign. I am overwhelmed especially by the generosity of those families that chose to give more this year to help make up for those who were unable to participate,” she said. Piedmont Education Foundation will continue to accept additional gifts in support of Piedmont’s schools at PiedmontEdFoundation.org. Funds raised through the Giving Campaign and other PEF fundraisers will be distributed to Piedmont School District for use in next school year’s budget, 2021-22. articles.text: Local and state lawmakers, representatives, and political leaders have released statements following the insurrection that unfolded in Washington D.C. on the afternoon of January 6. On the morning of January 6, supporters of President Donald Trump gathered for a “Save America” rally. During his speech, Trump claimed again falsely that the 2020 general “election was rigged.” By that afternoon, Congress had convened at the Capitol Building in a joint session to certify President-elect Joe Biden’s win. Soon after Trump’s speech ended, an estimated thousands of protestors gathered in front of the Capitol building and began toppling barricades and pushing past Capitol Police officers. Once past police, the rioters ran up to the Capitol’s steps, banged on doors, and attempted to break in through windows, the Washington Post reported. A mob broke at least one window and breached the capitol at approximately 2:15 p.m. Once inside, rioters ran through halls, tried to push through doors, and fought with police. “Then they were pounding on the door, so they told us to lie down on the marble floors which we did, and then there was a shot,” reported Congresswoman Jackie Speier of Hillsborough. At 2:20 p.m. PST, Rep. Speier tweeted “the Capitol has been breeched [sic]. We are in lock down!” At that time, Capitol Police ordered all staff, reporters and nearby senators into the Senate Chamber, which was sealed off and put on lockdown. Five people died and police made at least 52 arrests. No elected officials were harmed. The senate reconvened to complete the confirmation of Biden’s win, which was completed early the following morning. Gov. Gavin Newsom called the mob violence an “outright assault to our democracy” immediately after the events on January 6. “The people of California have spoken, and our congressional delegation should never have to fear for their lives to represent Californians,” Newsom said. “We are concerned for the safety of California’s congressional delegation and U.S. Capitol staff, and are reaching out to offer support in every way possible. President Trump must call for an end to this escalating situation, acknowledge the will of the people to bring President-Elect Biden to the White House and move immediately to a peaceful transition of power.” The same day, Senator Dianne Feinstein used social media platform Twitter to urge President Trump to “stop inciting violence with false claims of election fraud.” Trump did later condemn the violent acts of January 6, but many said it was too late, and that irrevocable damage had already been done. California Rep. Ro Khanna, along with many other democratic leaders, are echoing House Speaker Nancy Pelosi’s call to use the 25th Amendment to remove Trump from office. “I support the Speaker, whether it is impeachment or whether it’s the 25th Amendment, but what really needs to happen is a group of Republicans like Mitch McConnell need to go over to the White House and demand Trump’s immediate resignation and say the votes are there for an impeachment,” Khanna said. “That’s what happened in Richard Nixon’s case.” Congressman Eric Swalwell of Dublin, a member of the house Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence and of the House Judiciary Committee, demanded Trump’s immediate removal from office. “For the guarantee of our Republic’s survival, President Trump must be removed from office – either by the 25th Amendment or impeachment and removal in the Congress. President Trump can no longer defend our country or her ideals,” Swalwell said, adding that there must be an extensive investigation of how the Capitol was violently breached. Pelosi addressed the situation on Wednesday evening, January 7. “To those who strove to deter us from our responsibility, you have failed. To those who engaged in the gleeful desecration of this, our temple of democracy, American democracy, justice will be done,” she said. Many drew parallels to the strong police force that convened on the capitol in response to Black Lives Matter protests last summer. Rep. Barbara Lee of Oakland, who spoke the next day to KGO’s Kristen Sze regarding the events, said, “You can’t tell me that there’s not some systemic racism that we saw yesterday (January 6) in the disparities in how Black Lives Matter protesters would have been pushed back and how these protesters [were treated] because they’re Donald Trump protesters.” Rep. Eric Swalwell of Dublin House Speaker Nancy Pelosi of San Francisco “They [rioters] were there by the orders of this President; they were told to come to the Capitol and they were primarily white. You can’t tell me the response was equitable, because it wasn’t,” Lee said. San Francisco Mayor London Breed called the event “an attempted coup encouraged by the President.” Oakland Mayor Libby Schaff urged the public to “not lose faith in American democracy” and to “continue to push leaders to be more responsive to the American people, but also to not cross the line. On Monday, Democrats in the House of Representative introduced a single article of impeachment against the President, formally charging him with “incitement of insurrection” and making him the first president in American history to be charged with impeachment twice. The impeachment article states that Trump “willfully made statements that, in context, encouraged – and foreseeably resulted in – lawless action at the Capitol such as: ‘if you don’t fight like hell you’re not going to have a country anymore.” On Tuesday evening, January 12, Vice President Mike Pence said that he would not be invoking the 25th amendment to remove President Trump from office, and said “I will not now yield to efforts in the House of Representatives to play political games at a time so serious in the life of our nation.”

Bay Area lawmakers respond to Jan. 6 domestic attack on Capitol By Allyson Aleksey Local and state lawmakers, representatives, and political leaders have released statements following the insurrection that unfolded in Washington D.C. on the afternoon of January 6. On the morning of January 6, supporters of President Donald Trump gathered for a “Save America” rally. During his speech, Trump claimed again falsely that the 2020 general “election was rigged.” By that afternoon, Congress had convened at the Capitol Building in a joint session to certify President-elect Joe Biden’s win. Soon after Trump’s speech ended, an estimated thousands of protestors gathered in front of the Capitol building and began toppling barricades and pushing past Capitol Police officers. Once past police, the rioters ran up to the Capitol’s steps, banged on doors, and attempted to break in through windows, the Washington Post reported. A mob broke at least one window and breached the capitol at approximately 2:15 p.m. Once inside, rioters ran through halls, tried to push through doors, and fought with police. “Then they were pounding on the door, so they told us to lie down on the marble floors which we did, and then there was a shot,” reported Congresswoman Jackie Speier of Hillsborough. At 2:20 p.m. PST, Rep. Speier tweeted “the Capitol has been breeched [sic]. We are in lock down!” At that time, Capitol Police ordered all staff, reporters and nearby senators into the Senate Chamber, which was sealed off and put on lockdown. Five people died and police made at least 52 arrests. No elected officials were harmed. The senate reconvened to complete the confirmation of Biden’s win, which was completed early the following morning. Gov. Gavin Newsom called the mob violence an “outright assault to our democracy” immediately after the events on January 6. “The people of California have spoken, and our congressional delegation should never have to fear for their lives to represent Californians,” Newsom said. “We are concerned for the safety of California’s congressional delegation and U.S. Capitol staff, and are reaching out to offer support in every way possible. President Trump must call for an end to this escalating situation, acknowledge the will of the people to bring President-Elect Biden to the White House and move immediately to a peaceful transition of power.” The same day, Senator Dianne Feinstein used social media platform Twitter to urge President Trump to “stop inciting violence with false claims of election fraud.” Trump did later condemn the violent acts of January 6, but many said it was too late, and that irrevocable damage had already been done. California Rep. Ro Khanna, along with many other democratic leaders, are echoing House Speaker Nancy Pelosi’s call to use the 25th Amendment to remove Trump from office. “I support the Speaker, whether it is impeachment or whether it’s the 25th Amendment, but what really needs to happen is a group of Republicans like Mitch McConnell need to go over to the White House and demand Trump’s immediate resignation and say the votes are there for an impeachment,” Khanna said. “That’s what happened in Richard Nixon’s case.” Congressman Eric Swalwell of Dublin, a member of the house Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence and of the House Judiciary Committee, demanded Trump’s immediate removal from office. “For the guarantee of our Republic’s survival, President Trump must be removed from office – either by the 25th Amendment or impeachment and removal in the Congress. President Trump can no longer defend our country or her ideals,” Swalwell said, adding that there must be an extensive investigation of how the Capitol was violently breached. Pelosi addressed the situation on Wednesday evening, January 7. “To those who strove to deter us from our responsibility, you have failed. To those who engaged in the gleeful desecration of this, our temple of democracy, American democracy, justice will be done,” she said. Many drew parallels to the strong police force that convened on the capitol in response to Black Lives Matter protests last summer. Rep. Barbara Lee of Oakland, who spoke the next day to KGO’s Kristen Sze regarding the events, said, “You can’t tell me that there’s not some systemic racism that we saw yesterday (January 6) in the disparities in how Black Lives Matter protesters would have been pushed back and how these protesters [were treated] because they’re Donald Trump protesters.” Rep. Eric Swalwell of Dublin House Speaker Nancy Pelosi of San Francisco “They [rioters] were there by the orders of this President; they were told to come to the Capitol and they were primarily white. You can’t tell me the response was equitable, because it wasn’t,” Lee said. San Francisco Mayor London Breed called the event “an attempted coup encouraged by the President.” Oakland Mayor Libby Schaff urged the public to “not lose faith in American democracy” and to “continue to push leaders to be more responsive to the American people, but also to not cross the line. On Monday, Democrats in the House of Representative introduced a single article of impeachment against the President, formally charging him with “incitement of insurrection” and making him the first president in American history to be charged with impeachment twice. The impeachment article states that Trump “willfully made statements that, in context, encouraged – and foreseeably resulted in – lawless action at the Capitol such as: ‘if you don’t fight like hell you’re not going to have a country anymore.” On Tuesday evening, January 12, Vice President Mike Pence said that he would not be invoking the 25th amendment to remove President Trump from office, and said “I will not now yield to efforts in the House of Representatives to play political games at a time so serious in the life of our nation.”

Piedmont boys and girls, and existing Scouts can now begin signing up for the Scout Council’s Sea Scouts program, with an opportunity for adventures from to McCovey Cove to Angel Island, and possibly the Delta. The new vessel, the third iteration of the SSS Revenge, elicited high praise from veteran Piedmont Scouter Javier Jerez, who will head up the revitalized Sea Scout program. Standing on the boat in its berth at Ballena Bay in Alameda, he recently said. “It is just built like a tank. The boat has really good bones. It is really exciting, ” The donor, Jonarde Raab, put $25,000 into the boat with the intent of sailing it around the world. Jerez says the boat is easily worth double that now and is in really good shape. Raab made the donation with the condition that it would be used by the Scouts and not sold to fundraise for another boat or another program. This caveat suited the Scouts and Jerez, as the newest Revenge increases the range and potential of the program exponentially. New Piedmont Scouting Director Kate Benson is strongly looking forward to the time when the Scouts will be able to invite people on the boat. Current Covid restrictions preclude that. “We have the utmost gratitude to Jonarde Raab for his generous donation of the boat for use in our Sea Scouts program. There are a lot of different program opportunities in scouts, but [Sea Scouts] really provides some special and unique opportunities.” Describing the boat, Jerez said, “This design was very well respected as a blue water cruiser back in the late 70’s and early 80’s. It was what you wanted to go around the world in; this was ‘it!’” More than a few people have accomplished the feat of sailing around the world in one of these. “The Bay is one of the best places in the world to learn to sail. You get consistent strong winds and currents,” Jerez explained. He will be teaching Scouts navigational skills with excursions on the Bay, to include some night sails. Jerez also envisions sailing past the Golden Gate and going north to Drake’s Bay at Point Reyes for a possible overnight, and later possibly a weeklong trip on the Delta. In a future year it’s likely they will be among the hundreds of boats on the Bay during Fleet Week when the Blue Angels fly over San Francisco and over the Bay. Jerez has taken friends and scouts to Angel Island for an overnight camping trip. Not many Sea Scout programs exist, although the national program started at the same time as the Boy Scouts – in 1910. Piedmont’s program will now be able to draw an interest from high school girls and boys ages 14-20. “We are kind of like the Swiss Navy, because we are completely landlocked,” Jerez said with a laugh. “’Piedmont has a boat?’ people ask me.” The vessel be a place of learning. “Sailing has a huge learning curve – gigantic, never ending. The scouts will be learning about sail-trim, weather, piloting, coastal navigation, off-shore navigation, and more weather.” Jerez explained. articles.text: The Tule Elk State Natural Reserve can be found north of Tomales Bay State Park and the small town of Inverness in the Pt. Reyes National Seashore. Sunday’s High Surf Advisory along the California coast made for terrific wave-watching, while taking the near-five mile hike to Tomales Point put walkers next to herds of Tule Elk undisturbed by passersby. Taking the 9.7 out-and-back Tomales Point Trail heads to the northern most point on the Inverness side of Tomales Bay— overlooking remote stretches of beaches on the Pacific coast line to your left with Tomales Bay and The view of the remote Driftwood Beach along the Tomales Point Trail. You won’t find any tree cover on the Tomales Point Trail. Park officials advise to wear layered clothing to deal with the randomly changing weather on the coast. Staff Photos Herds of Tule Elk can be spotted at their reserve in the Pt. Reyes National Seashore on the Tomales Point Trail. the town of Dillon Beach to your right. The hike starts at Pierce Point Ranch, a historic farmstead of the Pt. Reyes Peninsula that has informative markers to describe the early dairy farming culture of the area. The near five mile walk to Tomales Point is in conjunction with the Tule Elk Reserve, there herds of male bulls, female cows, young male spikes, and baby calves. The ending is a bluff overlooking tide pools and a common array of birds: pelicans, cormorants, gulls, while red-tailed hawks and turkey vultures are often spotted looking for food as well. As for the main attraction, the Tule Elk, they are native to Central California and regarded as the smallest subspecies of elk. The Tule Elk were a big part of the Pt. Reyes National Seashore’s induction in 1976. At that time, the species faced local extinction due to hunting in the 1850s. In the fall of 1978, the National Park Service released 17 elk into the area after converting decommissioned farmland into a reserve. Now, park census recorders have estimated over 400 elk currently present in the Tomales Point region. It is important to note this trail’s qualities before would-be patrons venture on the 9.7 mile out-and-back walk: A popular destination due to the elk, we passed 133 people on our Sunday, 11 a.m. hike to Tomales Point and crossed another 68 on the way back to the car—making an average of slightly over 20 people per mile—meaning it’d be irresponsible to be without a protective face cover during a pandemic. Also, the area is located along the wind-swept region of Bodega Bay on the ridgeline of the Pt. Reyes National Seashore. Without any tree coverage, visitors should The bluff at the end of the Tomales Point Trail travels downward and overlooks tide pools and Bodega Bay to your right.

There are a lot of people having these conversations.” “The main goal is to get kids back into competition. That’s goal No. 1 at this point. Allow kids to have some semblance of normalcy is the goal,” added Central Coast commissioner Dave Grissom. Right now, only cross country would be given the green light to start competition once stay-athome orders are lifted. The inherent dilemma with reshuffling the CIF’s individual sports’ schedules comes with their overall planning this far. articles.text: These are dark, woeful, painful days (the pandemic, politics), but there’s a ray of sunshine if you’re a basketball fan, as I am. Jeremy Lin is a Golden State Warrior (again). You remember Jeremy Lin, right? Basketball fans certainly do, and many non-fans might. Eight years ago, there was no bigger star in professional basketball than Jeremy Lin. From obscurity, he became an international celebrity for what he did in February 2012, in New York City, the biggest American (and, arguably, world) stage of all. Really famous people (Barack Obama, Donald Trump, Spike Lee, et. al.) wanted to be his buddy. Documentary films were made of him. He gained fame and fortune. He was all of 23 years old. He created what became known as “Linsanity,” a phenomenon that dazzled the Big Apple and went stratospheric in the international world of sports and entertainment culture. For 12 games that month, Lin, a virtual nobody, became a sudden superstar, by leading the New York Knicks to many wins after the team had played terribly. Shortly thereafter, Lin came down to earth. He became injured and the Knicks didn’t exactly go overboard to try to retain his services after his Linsanity season ended. He bounced around with seven other NBA teams, never soaring to Linsanity levels again. Most recently, he played in China, where he was a star for a Beijing team. China, however, is where aging or underperforming NBA players go to try to revive their careers. Over the past weekend, the Warriors signed a deal with Lin and assigned him to their G-League team, the Santa Cruz Warriors. Frankly, it’s insulting that he’s being sent down to the G-League, which is like a training camp usually for marginal and inexperienced rookies. Lin has a lot of NBA experience and played well in China. Nonetheless, he’s going to have a chance to play for the Real Warriors again, his first NBA team after he wasn’t drafted by any team in 2010. The first time around with the Dubs, the 2010- 2011 season, he was mostly a benchwarmer and played very little. He eventually ended up with the New York Knicks in the Linsanity 2011-2012 season. We pro-Lin Warriors fans, however, can dream a little, can’t we? Already we hear some Dubs’ fans pooh-poohing the possibility of Lin becoming a Real Warrior again. Too old (32). Skills eroded. Too much competition on the Warriors’ roster. Can he really help the Warriors get back to elite status? That may all be true, but it’d be sweet if Lin became a Real Warrior again. The Bay Area, after all, is where he began his basketball career. He was a star on the Palo Alto High School team. It still puzzles me why Stanford, Cal, or UCLA never encouraged him to enroll. Palo Alto High is directly across the 101 freeway from Stanford. He had to “settle” for Harvard (yes, that Harvard, not exactly your typical collegiate basketball factory like Duke or Kentucky). H i s h o m e c o m i n g i s heart-warming to Warriors’ fans and the Bay Area’s large and diverse Chinese American/Asian American population. Born in Southern California to immigrant Taiwanese parents, he became the first Chinese American/Asian American in the NBA, a league dominated by African Americans. (There have been several other Chinese-from-China NBA players, the most famous being Yao Ming, who played for the Houston Rockets.) That’s one reason why I and other Chinese Americans and Asian Americans became Linsane. (Many nonAsians were also.) You know the stereotypes, don’t you? We folks of Asian descent are technological geeks, math and science wizards, conformist professionals, hard-working support staff, etc., but never a Superstar celebrity known practically worldwide! And never a professional basketball player, let alone one who for a month sucked up gobs of national and international attention. The racial-ethnic angle isn’t why Lin should play for the Real Warriors again. That decision should be made on the basis of his G-League performance, the team’s needs and the ultra-complicated financial and contractual protocols of the NBA and its teams. Call me sentimental, but given the racial-ethnic demographics of the Bay Area and of the Warriors’ fan base, his joining the Warriors would be a feel-good moment that we should all have right now, don’t you think? William Gee Wong, a Piedmont resident, is a retired syndicated journalist and author of Yellow Journalist: Dispatches from Asian America and Images of America: Oakland’s Chinatown.
articles.title: Bay Area native Jeremy Lin is back with the Warriors

articles.text: All entries ae due by January 31 Filoli House and Gardens in Woodside. Filoli House and Garden, located in Woodside, is conducting a haiku contest to complement its “Winters at Filoli” calendar of events. Winter at Filoli is a time of quiet reflection in the garden. Interested participants can submit a haiku inspired by Filoli’s winter garden for a chance to win a Household Plus Membership, as well as a beautiful gift basket of Filoli-approved goodies. “Late December and early January tend to be a period of heavy rains, and with that rain comes a washing of the plants and hardscapes,” Director of Horticulture Jim Salyards said. “There is a vibrancy to the bare branches of the deciduous shrubs and dark green leaves of the evergreens during the winter months. The brick paths and walls, the balustrades, and even the gravel paths seem even more prominent in the cool and wet weather.” You may submit up to three original poems. Poems should be in the general haiku format of three short lines of 5-7-5 syllables, or free-form haiku. They must be inspired by nature, in this case by Filoli’s winter garden. Three prizes are being offered. Prizes • First Place: Filoli Household Plus Membership and Gift Basket • Second Place: Filoli Individual Plus Membership • Best Under 18: Filoli Household Membership All entries should be submitted by midnight, January 31. Finalists will be announced on Filoli’s website on February 10. Winners will also be announced via Zoom on Valentine’s Day, February 14. Special guest judge and San Mateo County Poet Laureate Aileen Cassinetto will read the winning poem online on Valentine’s Day. To submit your haiku, visit https://filoli.org/haiku/.

articles.text: Dylan Walsh stars in The Stepfather. Movie review by Chris Honoré While The Stepfather is neither subtle nor shy, it does ratchet up serious tension as the film moves inexorably toward its predictable and harrowing conclusion. The story is familiar – a remake of the 1987 movie of the same name. It aims at that primordial fear that we don’t really know the people we’re close to until it may be too late. David Harris (Dylan Walsh), charming and smooth, inserts himself into the lives of a mother, Susan Harding (Sela Ward), and her three children. Susan is just coming off of a divorce and is vulnerable. The kids are teens and adjusting to a split family and weekends with dad. Suddenly they have a supportive guy around, someone who often insists that all he values in life is family. He tells them that his wife and daughter were killed in a car accident more than a year ago. The screenwriters do an interesting thing at the outset. They make it clear to the audience that Harris is a psychopath and pure evil in the guise of a wonderful guy. So, the first shoe is immediately dropped. What gives the film an unrelenting tension is that the audience is waiting for the second shoe to drop. The test of the film is how effective the filmmakers are in revealing to the unsuspecting family that Harris is a stone cold killer who is moving placidly among his victims with a wide smile and a loving, helpful persona. All the while small chinks – ever so subtle, ever so easily explained – in his behavior begin to appear. It’s chilling to watch. Walsh, as an actor, does a superb job in transforming his face from barely controlled rage to wide smiles in mere seconds. Susan, meanwhile, is oblivious. She’s in love. Her oldest son, Michael (Penn Bradley), however, begins to suspect that something is deeply wrong, though his girlfriend (Amber Heard) insists that it is all in his imagination. The audience knows he is right and it’s just a matter of time. The second shoe is about to fall. And it’s those minutes that make all the difference. As psych-horror films go, The Stepfather is well done. It’s a B-movie to be sure, one targeted at teens who unabashedly enjoy the genre and will surely turn out for this one. The Stepfather. Starring Dylan Walsh, Sela Ward, Penn Badgley and Amber Heard. Directed by Nelson McCormick. 1 hr., 41 min. Rated PG-13.

articles.text: Movie review by Chris Honoré Nanny McPhee was last seen in 2005 arriving to set right a dysfunctional family needing more than an intervention. They needed the McPhee magic, delivered by a snaggletooth, starched, ominous and mysterious nanny who arrives with magic at her fingertips and a cane to put things right. McPhee is a wonderful character, played perfectly by the gifted Emma Thompson. In the recent incarnation, Nanny McPhee Returns, written by Thompson, McPhee arrives at a bucolic farm in northern England. It’s the middle of World War II and children from London, which is being subjected to Germany’s blitzkrieg bombing, are sent across England to wait out the war, most in the safety of the English countryside. And so we are introduced to the Green children and their mother, Isabel Green (Maggie Gyllenhaal). The family is hanging on by a thread, financially and emotionally, while waiting for the father to return from the war. What is a normal state of chaos on the farm turns chronic when cousins Cyril (Eros Vlahos) and Cella (Rosie Taylor-Ritson), arrive from upper crust London in a chauffer-driven limousine. Dressed to the nines, they refuse to step out of the car, holding their noses, insisting they’ve arrived at a “poo and mud” museum. Everything is icky. They want to go home, and dig in their snobbish custom made heels, refusing to help out. Things are dire. Isabel’s brother-in-law (Rhys Ifans), a weasel, is trying to sell the farm to pay off gambling debts, the barley needs to be harvested, and a new batch of piglets must be sold to keep the family afloat. What to do? Enter Nanny McPhee, and just in time to teach the kids five life-lessons that will transform them and the farm, to the delight of all. The film is enhanced by CGI – pigs can and do fly and even synchronize swim. But at its center is a wonderful cast of characters who are both charming and engaging. Kids and adults will enjoy without reservation this entertaining film that delivers a heart-tugging ending after Nanny McPhee does indeed put everything right. Nanny McPhee Returns, Starring Emma Thompson, Maggie Gyllenhaal, Rhys Ifans and Maggie Smith. Directed by Susanna White. 1 hr., 49 min. Rated PG. articles.text: Movie review by Chris Honoré Nausicaa of the Valley of the Wind is extraordinary, not only as a high adventure story but as a work of art, its visual, handdrawn aesthetics are well beyond the trope known as the cartoon. Its animation is lush, detailed, and gorgeous. This feature was Hayao Miyazaki’s first major film in what would become the renowned Studio Ghibli astonishingly deepbench catalogue of dozens and dozens of animated films highly regarded throughout the world. The Nausicaa narrative is based on Miyazaki’s manga series of the same name and tells a tale of a planet that was reduced to a toxic, desiccated wasteland and poisoned jungle, the result of an apocalyptic war that took place some 1,000 years in the past. In the midst of toxic plants and huge insects, humans have survived and live on small inhabitable islands where they have fashioned an agrarian life that does possess some advanced technology. One of those islands is called the Kingdom of the Valley of the Wind, nestled in a mountain gorge. It is home to Princess Nausicaa (Alison Lohan), a courageous, adventurous young woman who travels on a jet-propelled glider that she uses for exploration. She possesses an affinity for animals and plants and can communicate with the Ohmu, whale-sized intelligent isopods that are the dominant species on earth. The film opens with Nausicaa on a trip to gather needed supplies and it is then that she meets Lord Yupa (Patrick Stewart), a wandering sage who has brought peace and wisdom to the valley. Arriving back home, she encounters a princess from another country who tells Nausicaa that the advanced, war-like nation of Tolmekia is planning to revive the doomsday machines, called the Giant Warriors, which had originally destroyed the planet. It is at this point that the very dense plot begins. There are two threads that hold this remarkable story together. One is its environmental point of view, made manifest through the efforts by Nausicaa to co-exist with nature. As well there is the heroic archetype as embodied in the Princess who defends and helps her people, displaying a willingness to endure physical pain and take great risks to achieve her objectives. She is fearless and brave, yet reluctant to turn toward violence, though capable of doing so. The plot is complex, layered, and requires a level of attention that may make it difficult for younger viewers to fully comprehend the story. Nausicaa of the Valley of Wind (1984). Animé – written and directed by Hayao Miyazaki. Fantasy and adventure. With the voices of Alison Lohan, Patrick Stewart and Uma Thurman. 1 hr., 35 min. Rated PG.

articles.text: Earl the Squirrel For the first time ever, I yield my column to a guest writer. He is a neighbor of mine who has a wealth of knowledge gained by perceptive experience and insight. He does not mince words, and will, therefore, say things that I never would. In sports, any outstanding player named Earl is knighted with the title “Earl the Pearl”. Please allow me to introduce my neighbor Earl the Squirrel. Q: Do you have any thoughts on the year 2020? Earl: Absolutely. I am glad you asked. 2020 began with every expectation of greatness. All the important musical organizations engaged the same shop – worn, completely predictable musical artistes. Those are the ones who bask in their own publicity but rarely live up to their press kits. The public appears to believe the publicity. Every performance gets a standing ovation. Q: How can you say this? Aren’t the top-notch performers better looking than ever before? Earl: Yep, that they are. The décolleté dresses women wear leave little to the imagination. Combined with leg-revealing skirts this makes their music more “all–encompassing“. Men simply can’t compete. So they eschew formal attire and stud their duds with safety pins or wear rabble-rousing shirts. It reminds me of the early days of the Russian revolution. Q: I try to avoid politics, but you opened the door. Isn’t revolution good? Earl: Mindless iconoclasm has its limits. Q: Well. I can see where this is going. Let me change the subject. Tell us about Michael Tilson Thomas, your friend from USC. Earl: Michael was the shining light in San Francisco for a long time. His final season was to be the best ever. The events of 2020 scuttled a beautiful season. But he won’t be forgotten. Q: And Beethoven and his 250th anniversary? Earl: He outlived his bad publicity. I read about him in the Piedmont Post of December 30. As soon as concerts begin again, we will hear more from him. Never fear. Q: Can you look into the future? Is our musical horizon a bright one? Earl: We need to get music education back in the schools big time. As I see it, the very existence of a healthy society depends on music education. The Greeks knew this. Why don’t our education administrators know the value of music? The cost is minimal but the societal rewards are great. I would even insist on music education in every prison. All humans have voices – so singing costs nothing. And I would call for community support. The Piedmont Center for the Arts has the right idea. Politicians could at least offer lip service – that would be a step in the right direction. I’d ask listeners to be enthusiastic, but also to listen critically. Sincere performers appreciate a standing ovation when it’s earned, not perfunctory. And finally, I’d encourage the audience to just come to concerts. It’s a lot of fun to be seen. Thanks, Earl. You have given me a lot to think about.

pages.text: Wednesday, January 13, 2021 21 Features Part 11 in a series By Will Adams Another important visual element of our built environment is signage. It is in many ways a lot like lighting, discussed in the last column. Both tend to stand out when done poorly and unrelated to their context. When designed well, both lighting and signage Signage seem to go unnoticed as they appear to fit right in, as if there were no other way they could have been designed. Besides providing necessary information to people on foot or in cars, appropriate signage can enhance and complement the architecture of a building or landscape of which it is a part. Walking around Piedmont, it is clear that the sensitive and understated use of signs pretty much everywhere contributes to the charm of the city. Like lighting, signage has both a functional requirement and an aesthetic character. Function is of course the first consideration: what is the sign’s purpose? In some cities very strict design review requirements for signs are problematic as they have resulted in a completely uniform, bland, lifeless array of signs, which are ironically hard to interpret or to decipher the required information. articles.text: This might sound weird to some, but I believe that when we look back on 2020, at some point many of us will see what a gift that year was. It wouldn’t hurt to start looking for the gifts now. In life, we attract what we look for. What we pay attention to, is what we get more of, i.e.: where attention goes, energy flows. And that’s not to say we should bypass the very real, very scary, and very threatening situations so many are dealing with. I’m not suggesting that we turn a blind eye. It’s a both/and. We can look at this past year and we can feel the weight of it. A lot of us have deeply felt the grief and fear that so much threat and uncertainty have brought, not just because of Covid but also the impact we feel as a country and in our communities because of the political environment. The recent upheaval by extremists in our capitol, and the heartbreak over the social inequities of our country, with ongoing racism, and double standards that people of color continue to face, are awful and difficult things to contend with. So how do we also make space for the good when so much is going sideways? We can turn our attention toward what we do have control over and that is: Noticing what is good. This is the perspective I am choosing to look for when I reflect upon how 2020 impacted the world of interior design and construction. We can notice what has happened to us as we have slowed down, how things that seemed stressful, and inconvenient, like the supply chain breaking on various levels, forced us to get creative: to upcycle, recycle, and go local, to pivot. We were forced into a slowdown because the supply chain wasn’t gushing at full force as we have come to expect. There is a slowdown, and I am looking at it as a blessing of sorts. If you know me, you know I’ve been emphasizing thoughtful consumption all along, choosing local, choosing high quality, breaking our dependency on cheaply made products from far away. (I mean YOU, Amazon!) At the beginning of this world-wide slowing down, we all saw for the first time in a long time how there was clean air because the factories that pump out these quickly available, easily acquired, cheap products were forced to shut down. So now, after almost 12 months of slowing down, this is a good time to consider how this past year has changed our consuming habits. What if these changes are for the better? In the high-end design world, this trend towards artisanal, quality, and local was bypassed on a grand scale for decades by the quickfix model so many industries had adopted. But like the lessons taught for years by Alice Waters, food activist and one of my heroines, the Slow Food movement – the trend toward slow consumption – has taken a stronger foothold this past year. And not just with food. It’s happening in my industry too. I could not be more delighted. It is a political, ecological, economic, and community-supporting act to focus our buying habits in this way. In recent decades the Internet changed how we feel about instant gratification. Wanting things fast, wanting them now, next day free shipping, at the press of a button. I found myself having the responsibility to educate clients, set boundaries, and let them know it’s up to us to change the world. Every drop in the bucket counts. pages.text: 24 Wednesday, January 13, 2021 Benefits of an all-electric home By Nate Redinbo An all-electric home is not as familiar as the increasingly popular electric car, but both innovations are important tools in the continued fight against climate change. Transportation is the No. 1 source of greenhouse gas emissions in the United States, followed closely by energy generation. Changing the way we use energy and drive can make a drastic change in emissions, both nationally and here in Piedmont. In an effort to reduce emissions stemming from energy usage, many California cities are advancing policies that encourage more electric appliances at home. In 2020, Berkeley banned natural gas in new buildings. Our other neighbor, Oakland, adopted a similar prohibition in December. Piedmont city staff introduced energy “reach codes” in 2020, which would reduce emissions coming from natural gas appliances over time. A second reading of the proposed reach codes will be brought to City Council in the future. Energy use in buildings is important because when a building is constructed, it generally remains standing for decades. A majority of Piedmont’s housing stock was constructed in the first half of the 20th century. Re-examining how we build and provide power in buildings and appliances can lead to big differences in emissions. Natural gas is less destructive than some other fossil fuels, but it still emits both carbon dioxide and methane when burned. Methane is more than 80 times more likely to trap heat in the atmosphere than carbon dioxide, so policymakers are trying to reduce natural gas usage as much as possible. Having homeowners switch their natural gas appliances to electric would mean fewer methane emissions and more “clean” energy usage. As the electrical grid continues to get greener over time, it uses energy generated from “greener” sources, including solar and wind power. This means that when appliances are turned on, instead of using natural gas, they would be powered by increasingly “green” power plants. Not only are electric alternatives more efficient, they can also save energy in the long term in most climate zones, including Piedmont’s. One aspect of home electrification that confuses people is how to go about doing it. Because many people grew up with gas stoves and furnaces, fewer people have heard of electric heat pumps or induction cooktops. Fortunately, appliances are continuously improving and installing an electric appliance is easier than one might imagine. Electric cooktops were long considered inferior to gas stovetops, but now options like induction cooktops are safer, faster, and easier to control than their gas counterparts. Besides ease of use and cost, using electric appliances limits the dangers associated with natural gas use. Natural gas usage, especially in the kitchen, can release toxic gases such as formaldehyde and nitrogen dioxide, which generally can lead to poor indoor air quality. During a time of COVID, living in a healthy home and environment is especially important. Electrification is a key to achieving a healthy and safe environment. The spacious dining room offered first-class dining on white linen tablecloths to visitors and residents in a room filled with potted palms. Large windows looked out to the park and a wide, open veranda offered outside dining. Victorians loved exotic plants, and Havens planted Queen palms, Canary Island date palms, cordyline trees (cabbage palms) The veranda at the Piedmont Clubhouse offered outside dining. and other exotics throughout the park. Just east of the clubhouse, Havens built a rustic teahouse. Stickwork formed the railings, posts and roof of this first teahouse. Thatch and later vines covered the roof, providing shade. That evening hundreds of small twinkling lights in the trees created a fantasy parkland for partygoers. Only the Clubhouse and the mineral spring grottoes were built at this time. articles.text: As California lags behind other states in COVID-19 vaccine distribution, Gov. Gavin Newsom has set a goal of administering 1 million doses by this weekend. To improve vaccination rates, mass drive-through vaccine distribution sites will be opening around the state, including one at the Oakland Coliseum. After discussions with the Oakland A’s and local healthcare providers, Alameda County officials will vote this week on opening a distribution site in the parking lot of the Coliseum. The date of the site’s opening has not been announced. The state is pushing to administer its stock of over 2.83 million doses of vaccine to healthcare workers and residents of longterm care facilities. “Those frontline workers — that’s why we want to vaccinate the vaccinators — so many of them are in those categories of vaccinators themselves, and those residents that are most vulnerable in these congregate facilities,” said Gov. Newsom in a press conference on Monday, January 11. According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, California has administered 782,638 doses as of January 11. While California possesses the most doses in the nation, it is one of only eight states with a vaccine distribution rate below 2,000 doses per 100,000 residents. According to the state’s vaccine distribution framework, Alameda County is part of Region II, a grouping that includes a wide swath of coastal Northern California from Santa Clara County to Del Norte County at the Oregon border. In all of Region II, the narrowest dataset provided by California health officials right now, almost 199,000 vaccine doses have been administered as of Sunday, January 10. In mid-December, the Alameda County Department of Public Health began administering its first vaccine doses. California has prioritized vaccine distribution based on several broad categories. The people that are now receiving the vaccine are healthcare workers and residents of long-term care facilities, a category that counts an estimated 3 million people. Next in line are individuals 75 years of age or older as well as people working in education, childcare, emergency services, food, and agriculture. The state believes this tier will begin receiving doses later this month. After that, vaccines will be available to people aged 65 to 74 years and people working in fields including transportation, logistics, the industrial sector, the commercial sector and critical manufacturing. This tier also includes people living in congregate settings, like the homeless or those in prison. Next, probably in the spring, vaccines will be administered to people aged 50 to 64 as well as people aged 16 to 64 with underlying health conditions. People working in sectors like defense, energy, communications, finance, and government operations will also receive the vaccine. The state estimates that the vaccine will be widely available to the general public beyond these specific groups by the summer or fall, although health officials noted that the timeline is subject to change. California is administering two different vaccines for free, one manufactured by Pfizer and another by Moderna. Both vaccines were granted emergency use authorization by the Food and Drug Administration late last year. Importantly, both vaccines require two doses administered several weeks apart. As of now, there is no statewide registry to sign up to be vaccinated. Healthcare workers should contact their employers about when they will receive the vaccine, while residents in longterm care facilities should contact their caretaker.

articles.text: Result: Tackled while running away; taken to jail Piedmont Police officers parked in the Ace Hardware parking lot for traffic surveillance on Grand Avenue had a surprise visitor. At 7:34 p.m. on Thursday, January 7, in the nearly deserted parking lot, a white Hyundai Sonata entered the parking lot and parked behind the patrol vehicle. The Hyundai remained parked for about 15 minutes as the driver, Christopher Vargo, 32, a transient, got in and out of the vehicle several times. Vargo then took a backpack from the vehicle and started walking away. Unaware that the Hyundai had been stolen, the officers got out of their car and asked Vargo who he was, where he was going, and why he was leaving the vehicle in the lot. As the officers were talking with him, a black Toyota Prius pulled up and two people got out. The Prius driver said he was the owner of the Hyundai, which had been stolen 20 minutes earlier from 1800 Lakeshore Avenue. The police called for backup, and a third Piedmont police officer arrived. While one officer was questioning Vargo, he started walking away on Grand Avenue and onto Sunnyslope Avenue. As the officers told him to stop, he became non-compliant and began walking aggressively toward one officer, a female. Another officer tackled the suspect. Vargo was arrested and transported to Santa Rita jail for possession of a stolen vehicle and resisting arrest.
